paragraphs.text: Wolfram syndrome-2 is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. As with other forms of Wolfram syndrome, the minimal criteria for diagnosis are insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and optic atrophy (El-Shanti et al., 2000; Mozzillo et al., 2014). WFS2 differs from WFS1 because it lacks diabetes insipidus and psychiatric disorders and includes bleeding upper intestinal ulcers and defective platelet aggregation (El-Shanti et al., 2000; Mozzillo et al., 2014).

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) reported a 17-year-old Caucasian girl born to parents who reported no consanguinity. They described her as the first Caucasian patient with WFS2. Recurrent bleeding upper intestinal ulcers had begun at 5 years of age. At 14 years, she was diagnosed with malrotation and partial duodenal intussusception and underwent resection of part of the duodenum with duodenal-jejunal anastomosis. At 16 years, she developed reduced visual acuity (20/40 right, 20/50 left) and dyschromatopsia. She had bilateral optic disc pallor with preserved pupillary light reflexes. Pattern visual evoked potentials were normal, and brain MRI showed normal optic nerve caliber. At 17 years, she developed nonautoimmune diabetes and started insulin. Further studies showed bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, slow intestinal transit, and entero-gastric bile reflux. Ocular findings were unchanged after 5 years of follow-up. Visual field testing, electroretinography, and OCT of the macula and retinal nerve fiber layer showed moderate bilateral optic nerve involvement. These findings were compatible with optic neuropathy, and optic atrophy was excluded. Platelets showed reduced, reversible aggregation in response to ADP and absent secretion in response to ADP. Aggregation in response to collagen, epinephrine, and ristocetin was normal. At 22 years, she had diabetes, optic neuropathy with preserved visual acuity, tinnitus, high-frequency hearing loss, bile reflux, slow intestinal transit, the platelet aggregation defect, and bleeding upper intestinal ulcers. Her heterozygous parents and brother were apparently healthy, but they also showed reversible defective platelet aggregation in response to ADP.

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) noted that in the earlier Jordanian WFS2 patients, a bleeding tendency and gastric ulcers had been observed in 79% and 90%, respectively, and defective platelet aggregation had been reported with collagen. Optic atrophy in those patients had been seen after childhood or described as 'asymptomatic.' The authors suggested that the ocular disease in the Jordanian patients was probably optic neuropathy rather than optic atrophy. If so, they argued, WFS2 might not be a subtype of Wolfram syndrome, since optic atrophy is a main diagnostic criterion. They proposed that the difference in platelet findings (ADP versus collagen) might reflect differences in experimental conditions or variability between patients.

It was also supported by an Italian patient with a homozygous deletion whose parents and brother were heterozygous carriers (Mozzillo et al., 2014).

paragraphs.text: Amr et al. (2007) studied 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with WFS2 mapped to 4q22-q25. They identified a homozygous missense mutation (E37Q) in the ZCD2 (CISD2) gene. The mutation also disrupted mRNA splicing, eliminating exon 2 and introducing a premature stop codon. The authors concluded that this aberrant splicing was the basis of the disorder. Screening of 377 probands with hearing loss found no mutations in the gene. The encoded protein, ERIS, localized to the endoplasmic reticulum but did not interact directly with wolframin. Lymphoblastoid cells from affected individuals had normal resting intracellular calcium. However, when stimulated with thapsigargin, they showed a significantly greater rise in intracellular calcium than controls.

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) identified a homozygous intragenic deletion of the entire CISD2 exon 2 in an Italian girl with WFS2. The deletion was found by failure to PCR-amplify exon 2 and by cDNA sequencing. SNP array analysis of the trio confirmed it and showed that her parents and brother were heterozygous carriers. The parents reported no consanguinity, and runs of homozygosity showed no parental relationship. However, microsatellite analysis supported a common ancestor.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2009) found that Cisd2-deficient mice had features suggestive of premature aging. Mitochondrial breakdown and dysfunction with autophagic cell death occurred before the earliest signs of nerve and muscle degeneration. Cisd2 localized mainly to the mitochondria. Mitochondrial degeneration worsened with age, and autophagy increased in parallel with the premature aging phenotype. The authors proposed that WFS2 is a mitochondria-mediated disorder.

paragraphs.text: Amr et al. (2007) found a homozygous G-to-C transversion at nucleotide 109 of the ZCD2 (CISD2) gene in affected members of 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome-2. The change predicts a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution at a conserved residue. The mutation also disrupted mRNA splicing, eliminating exon 2 and introducing a premature stop codon. The authors proposed this splicing defect as the basis of the disorder. Lymphoblastoid cells from affected individuals showed a significantly greater rise in intracellular calcium than controls after stimulation with thapsigargin.

checks.claim: Amr et al. (2007) found a homozygous G-to-C transversion at nucleotide 109 of the ZCD2 (CISD2) gene in affected members of 3 consanguineous Jordanian families with Wolfram syndrome-2.
checks.evidence_quote: A G-->C transversion at nucleotide 109 predicts an amino acid change from glutamic acid to glutamine (E37Q).
checks.explanation: The title says the mutation is homozygous, and the abstract says it was found in the 3 consanguineous Jordanian families.

checks.claim: The CISD2 nucleotide 109 G-to-C transversion predicts a glu37-to-gln (E37Q) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: A G-->C transversion at nucleotide 109 predicts an amino acid change from glutamic acid to glutamine (E37Q).
checks.explanation: The paper gives the same nucleotide change and E37Q prediction.

checks.evidence_quote: The mutation was found to disrupt messenger RNA splicing by eliminating exon 2, and it results in the introduction of a premature stop codon.

checks.evidence_quote: Lymphoblastoid cells from affected individuals show a significantly greater rise in intracellular calcium when stimulated with thapsigargin, compared with controls
checks.explanation: The paper reports a significantly greater thapsigargin-induced calcium rise than in controls.

paragraphs.text: Mozzillo et al. (2014) identified a homozygous intragenic deletion of the entire exon 2 of the CISD2 gene in an Italian girl with WFS2. Her features included diabetes mellitus, optic neuropathy, bleeding upper intestinal ulcers, sensorineural hearing loss, and defective platelet aggregation to ADP. The deletion was detected by failure to PCR-amplify exon 2 and by cDNA sequencing, and SNP array analysis confirmed it. Its maximum size was restricted to 2,050 bp between intron 2 and intron 3. The deleted region includes the codons for amino acids 102 to 106, within the 2Fe-2S domain. Her parents and brother were heterozygous carriers.
